title: Two Years In: A WKU Student Looks Back
paragraphs: When Amir Bekzhanov arrived in Uralsk two years ago, he had never lived away from home, had never managed his own finances, and had never had to make a doctor's appointment in Russian. He had been studying English since the age of twelve, but had rarely spoken it outside a classroom. Now, as he sits in the third-floor café of the WKU main building with a coffee he has learned to make last for two hours, he is thinking about everything that has changed — and, more surprisingly, about everything that has not.

"When I first arrived," he says, "I was completely overwhelmed. I had been expecting university to be difficult, but I had been imagining academic difficulty — complex lectures, heavy reading lists. What actually happened was more complicated than that. I couldn't read the washing machine instructions. I didn't know how to argue politely with a landlord. I was missing home and didn't know how to talk about it without feeling stupid." He pauses. "Nobody teaches you that."

Amir is now in his second year of Computer Science. He has completed six semesters of courses, has built a student timetable application that is being used by over thirty of his classmates, and has been working part-time as a tutor for first-year students since October. His English, which was already strong when he arrived, has become something different — not just more accurate, but more confident. He uses it to think, not just to communicate.

"I was studying English for years before university," he says, "but I was always translating in my head. Now I'm not doing that most of the time. I'm just thinking directly. I'm not sure exactly when that changed — it happened gradually. One day I noticed I had been writing an email in English for twenty minutes without once thinking about what the Kazakh would have been."

The change he describes is one that language researchers have been studying for decades: the point at which a second language stops being a foreign system and starts being a working one. For Amir, it seems to have happened through necessity rather than method. He was put in situations where English was the fastest route to a solution — technical documentation, international coding communities, his professor's preferred language for feedback — and he adapted. "I didn't do it consciously," he says. "I was trying to fix a bug or understand an error message. The language was just the tool."

He is sitting with his laptop open, as he almost always is. On the screen, there is a Python script that he has been debugging since the morning. He is also, simultaneously, replying to a message in Kazakh, thinking in Russian, and talking to me in English. This is, he says, completely normal. "My grandmother always asks me: which language do you dream in? And I tell her: I don't know. I dream in situations, not words." He smiles. "She doesn't find that as interesting as I do."

Two years in, Amir does not feel that he has arrived anywhere final. He knows more than he did, and he is more capable than he was, and both of these things are true in ways that are difficult to separate from each other. The language has shaped the knowledge and the knowledge has shaped the language. When he tries to explain something about computer science in Kazakh, he sometimes finds that the Kazakh words are not quite precise enough, and that he needs to borrow the English ones. When he tries to explain something about his childhood in English, he sometimes finds the opposite: that English does not have the right words for what he means, and that he has to invent something approximate.
"Both languages are incomplete," he says finally. "But together they're enough."

dialogue.speaker: Amir
dialogue.text: I've been thinking about how much has changed in two years. Two years ago I had never cooked for myself.

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: And now you're actually good at it. You made that beshbarmak for us last month — it was incredible.

dialogue.speaker: Amir
dialogue.text: My grandmother had been teaching me for years. I just hadn't been paying attention until I had to.

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: I think that's how most things work. You were learning the whole time. You just didn't know you were going to need it.

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: My relationship with English. I used to think in Kazakh and translate. Now sometimes I think directly in English — and then I have to translate the other way to explain it to my parents.

dialogue.speaker: Amir
dialogue.text: That's exactly it. The language has become part of how you think, not just what you say.

keyPhrases.context: "I was completely overwhelmed." = too much to deal with at once.
"It happened gradually." = slowly, bit by bit, over time.
"I didn't do it consciously." = without deliberate intention.
"Simultaneously, replying... thinking... talking." = all at the same time.
"The Kazakh words are not quite precise enough." = exact and specific.
"He has to invent something approximate." = close but not exact.
"He adapted." = adjusted to the new situation.
"Both languages are incomplete." = each lacks something on its own.

vocab.definition: feeling that something is too much to cope with
vocab.example: When I first arrived at university, I was completely overwhelmed.

vocab.definition: in a deliberate or intentional way; being aware
vocab.example: "I didn't do it consciously." — it happened without deliberate effort.

vocab.definition: at the same time as something else
vocab.example: He was simultaneously debugging, messaging, and talking.

vocab.definition: exact and accurate; stated clearly and without ambiguity
vocab.example: "The Kazakh words are not quite precise enough."

vocab.definition: close to the actual, but not completely accurate
vocab.example: When a word doesn't exist, you invent something approximate.

vocab.definition: to change or adjust to suit a new situation
vocab.example: He adapted to English by using it in real situations every day.

vocab.definition: a way or path taken to reach a destination
vocab.example: "English was the fastest route to a solution."

vocab.definition: happening slowly and steadily over time
vocab.example: The change was gradual — he didn't notice it happening.
